After-the-fact enforcement is fragile too: the Italian Garante's EUR 15 million ChatGPT fine was annulled by the Court of Rome in March 2026, on a question of which regulator was competent rather than on the merits.

'GPC succeeded once regulators defined its meaning' overstates. The GPC FAQ says 'GPC on its own does not create any legally binding obligations'. It gained legal force only where regulators said it must be honoured: by 15 January 2025, California, Colorado, Connecticut and New Jersey had issued guidance treating it as a legally binding opt-out. Reworded to that scope.

The AG's DNT finding rested on a secondary paraphrase from the GPC FAQ. The primary source was read: California AG, CCPA Final Statement of Reasons, Appendix E (2020). It says businesses have 'discretion' to treat DNT as a useful proxy, and that a required global privacy control must communicate the consumer's intent to opt out. This matches the substance. The primary is added and the wording aligned: DNT was left to business discretion rather than forbidden.
'One-bit preference' has no support in any cited source. It is dropped as unnecessary.

The CCPA §7025(b) quote is correct. §7025(b)(2) is what separates a valid signal from DNT: the mechanism must make clear that using the signal 'is meant to have the effect of opting the consumer out'.

Context, not an error: IEEE 7012's own introduction describes GPC requests as ones 'which website operators can obey or ignore at their discretion'. That framing understates GPC's legal force in the states above, so this record's GPC wording should not be copied from the standard.

fieldFixes.response: The difference claimed is legal form. In its 2020 CCPA rules California's Attorney General did not require businesses to treat Do Not Track as an opt-out, leaving that to their 'discretion', because a required signal must clearly communicate an intent to opt out of sale. GPC did gain legal force where regulators said it must be honoured (California, Colorado, Connecticut and New Jersey by January 2025), although GPC 'on its own does not create any legally binding obligations'. IEEE 7012 is a contract with records, but it too needs counterparties willing to honour it. P3P's history is covered in other slices of this study and was not re-verified here.

issues: All three quotes are verbatim (--check FOUND on 2026-09-23). Source 0's quote is the negotiation sentence. The response's 'any protocol that serves the purpose' is from the same abstract (FOUND).

'Depends on implementations not yet public' is out of date. On 20 May 2026 the MyTerms team published an individual Internet-Draft, draft-curtis-myterms-01, the 'MyTerms Contract Negotiation Protocol'. It specifies a concrete protocol: JSON agreements with hashed Markdown texts, EdDSA/JWS signing with DID keys, three attestation levels, an 'X-MyTerms-Agreements' HTTP response header, a /.well-known/myterms-configuration discovery file, and endpoints for storing and retrieving signed agreements. It has no IETF standing. At its CPDP workshop on 22 May 2026 the project showed demonstration person and entity agents, a live signing, and an embedded deployment (DataPal). It said a reference browser plug-in and an open-source reference implementation were still being built. The demo site anysiteorapp.com is public. The response is updated to reflect all this.

The point says record content is 'left open'. The full text of IEEE 7012 (free on IEEE Xplore, read for this check) partly fills this in. Cl. 5.2.4 fixes the record's content: terms, date, time stamp, identifiers and a unique contract ID. Cl. 5.4.4 requires identical, immutable copies and substitutable storage. Cl. 4.3 requires a version number or release date for each agreement. Only the format and storage location are open. The point is narrowed accordingly.

The standard itself supports the core of the counterpoint, and more strongly than the FAQ. Its HTTP header and JSON/RDF encodings appear only in informative Annex A ('All annex contents are to be considered informative'). Cl. 5.5 says 'Interoperability between systems is not a requirement of this standard'. Added.
The claim that the project acknowledges jurisdictional differences had no source. It is supported by the MyTerms FAQ, now added.

fieldFixes.point: Key mechanics are left open or only sketched: the format and location of agreement records, how parties move between agreements over time, and which protocol carries them.
fieldFixes.response: IEEE 7012 deliberately allows 'any protocol that serves the purpose'. It fixes what a record must contain, but offers header and JSON encodings only as informative examples, and states that 'Interoperability between systems is not a requirement of this standard'. MyTerms says the record format is 'an option left open', and that how parties change agreements is left to developers. A MyTerms-team individual Internet-Draft (draft-curtis-myterms-01, May 2026) proposes one concrete protocol: DID-signed JSON agreements, an X-MyTerms-Agreements header and a .well-known discovery file. But it has no IETF standing. At the project's May 2026 workshop, demonstration agents were shown while the open reference implementation was still being built. Auditability across vendors therefore depends on which protocol gets adopted. The project acknowledges that agreements will differ across jurisdictions with different contract laws.

issues: Both quotes are verbatim (--check FOUND on 2026-09-23).

The response is wrong that 'which agreement prevails ... is a question the standard's public materials do not resolve'. The normative text of IEEE 7012-2025 is free on IEEE Xplore, and cl. 5.2.1.3 addresses this directly: 'The individual’s agent shall specify that the individual’s chosen terms shall supersede any Terms of Use (TOU) or Privacy Policy.' Informative Annex B also describes a site's alternative term that 'would supersede their TOU/PP defaults'. The standard does claim precedence. What remains open is whether that clause holds in contract law against click-through terms the person has also accepted. No court has ruled on this.

The point says the IETF vocabulary says contracts 'can trump' preferences. The draft says they 'might override' them. Its example says such arrangements 'likely apply ... unless the terms of the arrangement explicitly say otherwise'. It is also a non-consensus working draft, not a finished standard. Reworded.
The IETF draft's own caveat ('unless the terms of the arrangement explicitly say otherwise') fits 7012's supersede clause, and this is worth noting in the response.

fieldFixes.point: A site's own terms of service may override a person's signal, and the IETF's draft AI-preference vocabulary itself says contractual agreements 'might override' statements of preference.
fieldFixes.response: This cuts both ways. It is why 7012 frames the person's terms as a contract rather than a preference. The standard requires the person's agent to 'specify that the individual’s chosen terms shall supersede any Terms of Use (TOU) or Privacy Policy'. The IETF draft itself allows that an arrangement can 'explicitly say otherwise'. Whether that clause beats a site's click-through terms the person has also accepted is a question of contract law the standard cannot settle, and no court has yet tested it.

issues: The quote is verbatim (--check FOUND on 2026-09-23). It only says that negotiation is 'outside the scope' of the standard, which is not the same as prohibiting it.

The action is wrong about what the merchant may do. It says the shop's agent 'cannot counter-propose' and 'can only accept one of the offered agreements or decline'. The normative text of IEEE 7012-2025 (free on IEEE Xplore) gives the entity three options in cl. 5.3.1: '(a) Accept the terms an individual presents from the structured and bounded list, (b) Respond to the individual with a single alternative set of terms from the structured and bounded list, (c) Reject'. Cl. 5.2.2 caps this: 'There shall be no negotiation beyond the single choice by either party.' Informative Annex A.1 gives an example: the entity counter-offers SD BASE-AT, and 'IEEE 7012 does not permit more than 1 round of negotiation'. So a single counter-offer of another standard-form agreement is allowed. Editing the text and further haggling are not.
Title 'no haggling' is broadly right but is sharpened to reflect the one permitted counter-offer.

fieldFixes.title: The merchant's agent accepts - no haggling over the text
fieldFixes.action: ILLUSTRATIVE. The shop's agent accepts SD-BASE as offered. Under IEEE 7012 it could instead have rejected the offer, or answered once with a single alternative agreement from the same standard roster, which Maya's agent would accept or refuse. It cannot rewrite the agreement's text, and there is no second round.
fieldFixes.supportInPublicMaterials: IEEE 7012 cl. 5.3.1: an entity may accept the proffered terms, respond with 'a single alternative set of terms from the structured and bounded list', or reject them. Cl. 5.2.2: 'There shall be no negotiation beyond the single choice by either party.' Informative Annex A.1 walks through one counter-offer and notes that 7012 'does not permit more than 1 round of negotiation'. The abstract puts party-to-party negotiation over terms out of scope.
